title: Jotter Manufacturers foil-imprint notebook: cost schedule, fixed vs. variable costs, CVP and pricing recommendation
participant_role: Accounting manager of Jotter Manufacturers determining costs for a new foil-imprint notebook
judge_role: Senior sales manager of Jotter Manufacturers who needs costs to set the price of the new notebook
scenario:
You are to assume the role of accounting manager of JOTTER MANUFACTURERS, a company that manufactures a variety of specialty notebooks that have increasingly gained popularity over the past year. The senior sales manager (judge) has asked for your help in determining costs so that prices can be set for a new notebook that features a foil imprint that will debut on the market.

JOTTER MANUFACTURERS found that because of the specialty and unique design of its notebooks, it usually produces a range of notebooks, depending on model, of 10,000 to 30,000 notebooks per model per year. Because this notebook has yet to be advertised, the optimal quantity to produce is yet to be determined, but a competitor has a similar product on the market retailing for $4.75.

You will complete the cost schedule, and explain your work to the senior sales manager (judge).

[Cost schedule table: Number of notebooks produced 10,000 / 20,000 / 30,000, see exhibits]

When you explain the total cost per unit to the senior sales manager (judge), you must also explain the following:
- Types of variable costs that would be included in manufacturing these notebooks.
- Types of fixed costs that would be included in manufacturing these notebooks.
- The nature of overhead and operating costs.
- Why financial information is important in the pricing function.

Finally, you must make a recommendation and provide a rationale for the quantity to produce and pricing per unit.

You will present your work to the senior sales manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the senior sales manager's (judge's) office. The senior sales manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the work and have answered the senior sales manager's (judge's) questions, the senior sales manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Based on your cost schedule, should we consider a quantity of 40,000 or more?
How do you think customers may be influenced if our prices are higher than our competitors for a similar product?

solution.overview: A strong answer completes the schedule by holding variable cost at $1.50 per unit and fixed cost at $19,000 total, showing total cost per unit falling from $3.40 at 10,000 units to $2.45 at 20,000 and $2.13 at 30,000. It explains which costs are variable and fixed, distinguishes overhead from operating costs, uses CVP logic to recommend a higher volume (30,000) priced at or slightly below the competitor's $4.75, and explains how price affects customer buying behavior.

answer: Variable cost per unit = $15,000 / 10,000 = $1.50 and stays $1.50 at every volume
Total fixed costs stay $19,000 at every volume; fixed cost per unit = $1.90, $0.95 and $0.63
Total cost per unit: $3.40; $2.45; $2.13
Variable costs change in total with volume but stay the same per unit ($1.50 here)
Examples: paper, covers, foil for the imprint, binding wire or glue, packaging
Direct labor wages for production workers paid per hour or per unit
Fixed costs stay the same in total no matter how many notebooks are made ($19,000 here)
Examples: warehouse or factory rent, equipment rental or depreciation on the foil-stamping machine, insurance, salaried supervisors
As volume rises the fixed cost per unit falls, from $1.90 to $0.63
Overhead costs are more static and relate to general business functions, such as accounting staff salaries and facility costs
Operating costs are the materials, labor and machinery used to make the product or deliver the service
Both must be covered by the selling price for the notebook to be profitable

by_task.task: Why financial information matters for pricing
answer: Pricing needs a full picture of every cost tied to making the product
Only then can the price be set to cover cost and earn the proper profit margin
Cost data also shows how the competitor's $4.75 price compares to our cost at each volume
CVP analysis shows how changes in cost and volume affect net income; here higher volume lowers fixed cost per unit and raises profit per notebook
Recommend producing 30,000 notebooks, the top of the normal range, at a total cost of $2.13 per unit
Price at or slightly below the competitor's $4.75, for example $4.49 to $4.75, giving a margin of about $2.36 to $2.62 per notebook
Break-even at a $4.75 price = $19,000 / ($4.75 minus $1.50) = about 5,846 notebooks, well below any planned volume
Lower volume (10,000) would leave only about $1.35 of margin per unit at $4.75 and is less profitable

calculations.label: Variable cost per unit
steps: $15,000 / 10,000 notebooks = $1.50 per notebook (constant at all volumes)

calculations.label: Total costs and total cost per unit

judge_question_answers.question: Based on your cost schedule, should we consider a quantity of 40,000 or more?
answer: On paper, yes: at 40,000 the fixed cost per unit falls to $0.475 and total cost per unit to about $1.98
But 40,000 is above our normal 10,000 to 30,000 range for a model, and the notebook has not been advertised yet, so demand is unproven
Unsold notebooks tie up cash in inventory; fixed costs might also step up (extra space, machines) beyond the current range
Start at 30,000 and expand once sales data confirms demand

judge_question_answers.question: How do you think customers may be influenced if our prices are higher than our competitors for a similar product?
answer: Price is a major factor in buying behavior; many customers will choose the cheaper similar product
A higher price can work only if customers see added value: the foil imprint, quality, brand reputation or design
Other influences include convenience, availability, promotion and peer or social influence
Since our cost is $2.13 to $3.40, we have room to match or beat $4.75 and still earn a healthy margin

key_concepts.definition: A cost that changes in total in proportion to the number of units made but stays constant per unit. Variable cost per unit = Total variable cost / Units.
A cost that stays the same in total regardless of volume, such as rent or equipment rental. Fixed cost per unit = Total fixed cost / Units, so it falls as volume rises.
Variable cost per unit plus fixed cost per unit, or Total cost / Units produced.
A tool that shows how changes in costs and volume affect net income. It helps choose production quantity and price.
The volume where total revenue equals total cost. Break-even units = Fixed costs / (Selling price per unit minus Variable cost per unit).
Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit; the amount each unit contributes to covering fixed costs and then profit.
Static costs tied to general business functions rather than a specific product, such as accounting staff and facility costs.
The materials, labor and machinery costs used to make a product or deliver a service.
A record that accumulates the direct materials, direct labor and overhead costs of one specific job or product batch.
Setting a price by adding a desired profit margin to the full cost per unit, then checking it against competitors' prices.
Influences on what customers buy, including price, perceived value and quality, brand, convenience, promotion and social influence.

notes: The PDF solution completes the cost schedule; its 30,000-unit fixed cost per unit is misprinted as '$.063' where $0.63 is correct ($19,000 / 30,000 = $0.6333, total cost per unit $2.13). The PDF solution gives suggested points for variable costs, fixed costs, financial information, the CVP recommendation, overhead and operating costs, but no printed answers to the two judge questions and no specific quantity or price; the 30,000-unit recommendation, price range, margin figures, break-even calculation and judge question answers are model answers derived from the schedule. The evaluation form header for the Judge's Evaluation Instructions page is misprinted 'District Event #1'.
